title: A large, long-lived, slowly-expanding superbubble across the Perseus arm

paper_content.abstract: Stellar feedback is a crucial mechanism in galactic evolution, as demonstrated by the widespread bubbles observed with JWST. In this study, we combine data from Gaia and LAMOST to obtain a sample of young O-B2 stars with full three-dimensional velocity information. Focusing on the largest known superbubble in the Milky Way, we identify groups of O-B2 stars at its periphery, exhibiting a transverse velocity of 25.8 km s−1 and an expansion velocity of 6.2 km s−1. Using these velocities, we calculate a crossing time t_cross ≈ 20 Myr and an expansion timescale t_expansion ≈ 80 Myr. We estimate a survival timescale t_survival ≈ 250 Myr and a supernova interval t_SN ≈ 0.1 Myr. Together with the Galactic shear timescale t_shear ≈ 30 Myr, these values satisfy t_SN < t_shear < t_survival. The energy and momentum from supernovae are sufficient to sustain the bubble’s growth against ambient pressure. This indicates that repeated supernovae replenish energy faster than shear and turbulent distort the cavity. Our analysis classifies the Giant Oval Cavity as a large, quasi-stationary superbubble, similar to the Phantom Bubble observed by JWST, stabilised by the interplay between stellar feedback and Galactic disk dynamics.
paper_content.introduction:
The structure and kinematics of spiral arms are fundamental to understanding the formation and evolution of the Milky Way1. Spiral arms play a critical role in star formation by concentrating gas and dust into regions of high star-forming activity2–4. Investigating these structures provides key insights into the Galaxy’s overall dynamics and the processes driving its evolution5–8. Both observational studies and theoretical models suggest that spiral arms are dynamic and transient features that significantly influence the spatial distribution and motion of stars and interstellar matter9,10.

Star formation in the Milky Way begins with the collapse of molecular clouds, but this process is strongly regulated by stellar feedback11–13. Stellar feedback disrupts molecular clouds, thereby influencing the efficiency of star formation14,15. It also injects energy into the interstellar medium (ISM), sustaining turbulence and driving large-scale processes within the ISM16–18. The impact of stellar feedback is particularly evident in the widespread presence of bubbles observed throughout galactic disks, as recently highlighted by James Webb Space Telescope (JWST) observations19. The size distribution of the bubbles detected by JWST exhibits a secondary peak and a trailing extension at large radii, with these features becoming more pronounced at greater galactocentric distances20. However, their physical properties remain poorly understood due to observational limitations. Superbubbles in the Milky Way, particularly those in the Solar neighborhood, thus provide rare, kinematically resolved benchmarks for studying superbubble evolution.

The Sun is located within a superbubble known as the Local Bubble, which is associated with the Local Arm of the Milky Way21–24. By analyzing the three-dimensional (3D) distribution and motions of young stars, dust, and gas, we can identify large-scale structures such as superbubbles. These structures are shaped by the combined effects of stellar winds and supernova explosions, offering valuable insights into the feedback mechanisms that sculpt the ISM and influence the evolution of spiral arms. Despite their importance, comprehensive studies of superbubbles in spiral arms beyond the Local Arm remain limited. Recent advancements in observational astronomy, particularly through large-scale surveys such as Large Sky Area Multi-Object Fiber Spectroscopic Telescope (LAMOST)25,26 and Gaia27,28, have significantly enhanced the accuracy of stellar position and velocity measurements in the Milky Way. These improved datasets have deepened our understanding of spiral arm structures and underscored the role of young massive stars as key tracers of Galactic dynamics. In particular, the Perseus arm—one of the Milky Way’s major spiral arms and the closest spiral arm in the outer Galaxy—has garnered attention due to its complex interactions and unique kinematic properties.
paper_content.results:
O-B2 stars in the Perseus arm
We have compiled a comprehensive catalog of 369 very young (age < 20 Myr), massive O- and early B-type (O-B2) stars, using data from the LAMOST and Gaia surveys. These stars are associated with the Perseus arm, located within 0.5 kpc of the arm’s model in the Galactic XY plane. The spatial distribution of these stars exhibit clear clustering, corresponding to the structure of the Perseus arm, as shown in Fig. 1. The 3D positions and velocities of these stars provide significant insights into the kinematic properties of the Perseus arm and the underlying mechanisms that influence the spatial distribution and motion of stars and interstellar matter.

In the outer Galaxy, the Perseus arm is primarily traced by six prominent OB associations, spanning the Cassiopeia, Perseus, Auriga, Gemini, and Orion regions. The average peculiar velocity of stars within the Perseus arm is ~16 km s−1 in the XY plane, consistent with velocities observed in high-mass star-forming regions via maser measurements29. These peculiar motions allow us to explore dynamic trends within each OB association. Our analysis reveals the presence of the largest known superbubble in the Milky Way, referred to as the Giant Oval Cavity30. This structure spans across the Perseus arm, with a diameter exceeding 1 kpc. It is primarily bordered by the Cassiopeia and Auriga OB associations in the Galactic plane, while the Perseus OB association lies below the plane.

The Giant Oval Cavity is a slow-expanding superbubble
The Giant Oval Cavity extends across Galactic longitudes of ~100° to 150°, as shown in Fig. 1. Within this region, at |Z| < 100 pc, the Cassiopeia and Auriga Peninsula groups exhibit coherent XY motions directed outward from the cavity. This pattern strongly suggests an expansion phase for the superbubble. The observed stellar velocities result from a combination of their peculiar velocities and the expansion velocity of the surrounding cavity. To quantify these motions, we calculated the median velocities of the Cassiopeia and Auriga Peninsula groups and decomposed them into two components: a shared peculiar velocity and two oppositely directed components representing expansion from the cavity center. This decomposition is depicted in the right panel of Fig. 1. From our analysis, we derived an expansion velocity of v_expansion ≈ 6.2 ± 2 km s−1 and a shared peculiar velocity of v_parallel ≈ 25.6 ± 3 km s−1. The expansion velocity of the Giant Oval Cavity is consistent with measurements for the Local Bubble, which has an expansion velocity of ~5.5 km s−1 10. However, the Giant Oval Cavity is significantly larger, with a diameter of ~1 kpc compared to the ~200 pc diameter of the Local Bubble23.

In Fig. 2, we provide an edge-on view of the selected O-B2 stars. The Auriga peninsula, Perseus, and Cassiopeia OB groups form a continuous arc-like structure. The Auriga peninsula group is predominantly located near the Galactic plane, at Z ≈ 0, while the Perseus group is situated below the plane, at Z < 0, forming the southern segment of the Giant Oval Cavity. The Cassiopeia group exhibits a vertical distribution rising to the plane. This arc is primarily found on the southern side of the Galactic plane, extending to ~Z ~ −270 pc at its southernmost point, which is significantly higher than the typical scale heights of the Milky Way’s molecular gas disk, estimated to be 40–70 pc31–33.

Additionally, Fig. 2 shows the vertical velocity field associated with this large arc. Our analysis reveals a consistent vertical velocity pattern, with minimal oscillatory behavior. The O-B2 stars in the Auriga Peninsula group exhibit near-zero vertical velocities, while those in the Perseus group have notably negative velocities, indicating a rapid outward movement away from the Galactic plane. The Cassiopeia group shows a clear gradient in vertical velocities, with stars moving away from the plane at decreasing speeds as their distance from the Galactic plane decreases. A comparison of the vertical velocity and positional distributions reveals a striking agreement, with no discernible phase difference, suggesting that the arc is in a stable expansion phase. The estimated vertical expansion velocity of the superbubble is ~8.5 km s−1, which is comparable to its horizontal expansion velocity.

The Giant Oval Cavity, identified as a ~1 kpc scale region with reduced dust density30, is likely the largest known superbubble in the Milky Way disk. It represents an extreme example of stellar feedback-driven structures in disk galaxies. Interest in such large superbubbles has grown considerably following the identification of many similar features in external galaxies like NGC 62820. Several nearby stellar groups—specifically the Cassiopeia, Perseus, and Auriga Peninsula—exhibit positions and motions consistent with expansion driven by feedback from this cavity. In contrast, other groups along the Perseus arm, including Auriga, Gemini, and Outer Orion, show no evidence of such organized expansion. The absence of coherent radial motion in these groups, combined with the precise geometric alignment of expanding stars along the cavity boundary, suggests that these expansion patterns are not the result of random Galactic disk dynamics. Instead, they appear to be a direct consequence of the cavity’s influence. This disparity suggests a direct link between the ISM structure and the dynamics of associated stellar populations.

Observational data reveal a coherent expansion pattern, an organized velocity structure, and spatial undulations along the cavity’s boundary. These features support the interpretation of the cavity as a uniformly expanding superbubble. With an approximate diameter of 1 kpc and a current expansion velocity of ~6.2 km s−1, its estimated dynamical age, based on a simple R/v calculation, is approximately t_expansion ≈ 500 pc / 6.2 km s−1 ≈ 80 Myr. This makes it one of the oldest known superbubbles in the Galaxy, approximately four times older than the Local Bubble.

Theoretical framework for bubble stability
We propose that the Giant Oval Cavity belongs to a class of quasi-stationary bubbles whose boundaries are sustained by a dynamical balance between external gas inflow and energy input from supernovae occurring within the cavity. The cavity is sufficiently large that numerous supernovae are expected to explode inside it before Galactic turbulence and shear can erase the structure. In galactic disks, molecular gas has a typical velocity dispersion of ~4 km s−1 34. This velocity sets the rate at which turbulent gas flows can erode bubble boundaries. The corresponding survival timescale of a bubble is given by
t_survival = l_bubble / σ_v,disk (1)
where l is the characteristic size (i.e., diameter) of the bubble and σ_v,disk is the velocity dispersion of the surrounding medium. Applying this to the Local Bubble and the Giant Oval Cavity yields:
t_survival,Local Bubble ≈ 50 Myr (2)
t_survival,Giant Oval Cavity ≈ 250 Myr (3)

A bubble can retain its structure if a supernova explodes within it before it is eroded by turbulence. To estimate the supernova timescale, we assume a surface density of 5 M⊙ pc−2 35 and a gas depletion time of 2.5 Gyr 36 for the solar neighborhood. This implies a star formation rate of 2 M⊙ pc−2 Gyr−1. Assuming one supernova occurs per 150 M⊙ of star formation37, the local supernova rate is:
n_SN = 0.01 pc−2 Gyr−1 (4)

The time between supernova events within a bubble of size l_bubble is then given by:
t_SN = 1 / (l_bubble^2 * n_SN) (5)

Substituting characteristic sizes gives
t_SN,Local Bubble ≈ 2.5 Myr (6)
t_SN,Giant Oval Cavity ≈ 0.1 Myr (7)

t_SN ≪ t_shear implies feedback-dominated expansion, radial growth might become filled with dense gas before the next supernova can occur. However, larger bubbles—often located in the outer regions of galaxies—remain stable over extended periods.

The stability of the Giant Oval Cavity involves two primary criteria: temporal and energetic. We compare the supernova replenishment time, t_SN, with the timescale for differential rotation to distort the cavity, t_shear ≈ 30 Myr 41, and with the turbulent erosion time, t_survival. Supernovae must recur on a timescale shorter than both competing processes. Our calculated values, t_SN < t_shear < t_survival, meet this condition, indicating that feedback events are sufficiently frequent to prevent the bubble’s disruption. The combined energy and momentum input from supernovae must be sufficient to create the cavity by overcoming the gravitational binding energy and turbulent pressure of the ambient gas, and to offset radiative losses to maintain the cavity’s expansion over time. As detailed in the Methods, the Giant Oval Cavity requires ~400 supernovae to be powered. Our estimated supernova loading of the system satisfies this requirement, confirming that the energy and momentum budgets are ample. Meeting both the temporal and energetic criteria indicates that the Giant Oval Cavity is a long-lived, feedback-driven structure undergoing quasi-stationary expansion. In this regime, Galactic shear deforms the cavity significantly without erasing it completely, while the bubble evolves through concurrent expansion, contraction, and distortion. Its boundary maintains a dynamical equilibrium between shear forces, supernova feedback, and turbulent gas inflow. This explains the irregular boundaries seen in simulations (Fig. 3).

Several additional factors contribute to this picture. The bubble’s low-density interior likely reduces star formation rates compared to Galactic averages, potentially decreasing internal supernova rates. However, triggered star formation at cavity edges counteract this by enhancing stellar birth in compressed shells, which would further shorten t_SN. This aligns with observations showing elevated star formation rates in the Giant Oval Cavity region 42,43, consistent with the feedback-triggered star formation scenario.

Moreover, bubbles exceeding the Milky Way’s gas scale height (~100 pc) develop chimneys that vent hot gas vertically. Although t_SN ≪ t_shear implies feedback-dominated expansion, radial growth might halt when cavities surpass this scale height. For the Giant Oval Cavity, vertical venting converts radial momentum into vertical outflows, limiting lateral expansion while maintaining structural coherence through continuous feedback. Heat conduction44 also contributes to energy loss, but for larger structures, the relevant surface area—approximately r_bubble * h_disk —is proportionally smaller relative to their volume, reducing the overall impact.

Observations of young OB stars located beneath the cavity reveal vertical velocities directed away from the Galactic plane, consistent with momentum injection from recent supernovae. This supports a feedback cycle in which massive star explosions initially clear surrounding gas to create the cavity, while subsequent shockwaves compress nearby clouds, triggering new star formation. Later generations of supernovae from these young stars then replenish the system with energy, sustaining its expansion. This process aligns with our discovery of the ~10 Myr-old clusters observed along cavity edges, whose velocities match feedback-driven gas motions. We have conducted a detailed calculation of the number of supernovae required to form and maintain the Giant Oval Cavity. Accounting for the combined effects of energy injection, radiative loss, and ISM interaction, we estimate that ~400 supernovae are necessary. This estimate aligns with predictions from the Kennicutt–Schmidt relation45 for star formation on kiloparsec scales. A complementary estimate, scaling the Local Bubble’s ~20 supernovae24,46 by the cavity’s fivefold larger radius, yields about 500 supernovae—in close agreement with our detailed calculation. These feedback processes inject significant momentum into the ISM, driving large-scale structures such as gas chimneys that redistribute material vertically and may play a key role in shaping the interface between the Milky Way’s disk and halo.

In summary, large bubbles like the Giant Oval Cavity reach a quasi-stationary state where their boundaries are shaped by a dynamical balance between mass inflow, galactic shear, and internal supernovae. Shear continuously deforms the structure, while supernovae within the cavity counteract this by pushing material outward, maintaining a quasi-stationary boundary. These findings match galaxy-scale simulations showing that large cavities become long-lived, dynamically evolving structures capable of migrating within host galaxies. This framework provides a clear explanation for the nature of giant cavities such as the Phantom Bubble recently observed by JWST.
paper_content.methods:
Data and sample selection
This study utilizes data from LAMOST DR9 v1.0 26, which includes both low- and medium-resolution spectra obtained by LAMOST between October 2011 and June 2021. For this work, we focus on the low-resolution catalog, which contains over 10 million spectra. The low-resolution spectra have a resolution of R ~ 1800 and cover the optical wavelength range from 3800 to 9000 Å. Additionally, we incorporate data from Gaia DR3 28, which provides astrometric solutions and broad-band photometric measurements (G, G_BP, G_RP) for ~1.5 billion sources.

We selected O- and early B-type stars from the combined LAMOST and Gaia datasets. First, we cross-matched these datasets using a 1.5″ search radius. We then filtered stars with parallax uncertainties smaller than 20%. Distances were calculated from Gaia DR3 parallaxes using a Bayesian approach50,51, with the posterior probability given by:
p(d|ϖ) = d^2 exp(−1/2 * (ϖ - ϖ_zp)^2 / σ_ϖ^2) p(d) (8)
where σ_ϖ and ϖ_zp are the uncertainties and global zero-point offset of Gaia parallaxes, respectively, and p(d) is the prior on the space density distribution of the stars. We adopt a zero point of ϖ_zp = −0.026 mas from ref. 52, and the Galactic structure model from ref. 53 as the prior.

In the initial phase of our analysis, we excluded late-type main-sequence stars using the Gaia color-‘absolute’ magnitude diagram. The term ‘absolute’ magnitude here refers to a magnitude that accounts for the distance modulus but does not include corrections for interstellar extinction. It is calculated as G − 5 log d + 5, where d denotes the distance. As shown in the left panel of Fig. 4, we systematically removed late-type stars based on their observed colors and ‘absolute’ magnitudes. We retained only stars located above the B5V extinction curve, refining our sample to 57,375 stars.

A significant portion of the sample consisted of late-type giants. The lack of extinction corrections led to some overlap between early B-type main-sequence stars and redder giants. To further refine the selection, we calculated spectral line indices from the LAMOST spectra for these stars. We computed indices such as Ca II K, Hδ, CN, Ca 4227, G4300, Hγ, Fe 4383, He 4388, Fe 4531, Hβ, Ca 4455, He 4471, Fe 4531, He 4542, Fe 4668, Hβ, Fe 5015, Mg 1, Mg 2, Mgb, Fe 5270, Fe 5335, Fe 5406, and Fe 5709 54,55. To derive spectral line indices, we first identify the line of interest and select two continuum regions on either side of it. A linear fit is then applied to the flux values in these regions to establish the pseudo-continuum level. Finally, the line index (i.e., equivalent width) is computed by integrating the flux difference between the observed spectrum and the pseudo-continuum across the line’s wavelength range. Using machine learning techniques, specifically a random forest classifier, we identified OB stars among the candidates. Cross-referencing with the Simbad database, we selected 7873 stars with identified spectral types, including 3529 OB-type stars and 4344 stars of other types. We then trained a random forest classifier with spectral indices as inputs and spectral types as outputs. The distinct spectral line features of OB stars allowed the classifier to achieve an accuracy of 97%. Applying this classifier to the remaining candidates, we identified a final sample of 19,600 OB-type stars.

The primary objective of our study is to isolate very young (with ages t < 20 Myr) O- and early B-type stars (O-B2) to trace the superbubble structure of the Milky Way. For this purpose, we calculated atmospheric parameters for the 19,600 OB stars identified through spectral line indices using the HOTPAYNE pipeline56. As shown in the right panel of Fig. 4, the majority of the selected OB stars are main-sequence stars with temperatures exceeding 10,000 K. We specifically focused on stars earlier than B3 in spectral type, with effective temperatures T_eff > 19,000 K. This rigorous selection process resulted in a final sample of 1608 unique O-B2 stars.

Three-dimensional position and velocity
To determine the radial velocities of the refined O-B2 star sample, we analyzed their spectra obtained from the LAMOST telescope. Using theoretical template spectra for OB stars provided by TLUSTY57, we performed spectral fitting in the blue wavelength range (4000–5400 Å). This allowed us to accurately derive the line-of-sight velocities for each OB star. To estimate the uncertainty in radial velocities, we used a Monte Carlo (MC) method based on the spectral uncertainties reported by LAMOST. Specifically, we added normally distributed noise to the flux values based on their respective errors, recalculated the radial velocities 100 times, and derived the standard deviation of the results as the radial velocity uncertainty.

By combining the distances calculated from Gaia DR3 parallaxes, the radial velocities obtained from LAMOST, and the positional and proper motion data from Gaia DR3, we derived the three-dimensional positions (X, Y, Z) and velocities (V_x, V_y, V_z) for every star in the sample. In this coordinate system, the X-axis points towards the Galactic center, the Y-axis aligns with the direction of Galactic rotation, and the Z-axis points towards the North Galactic Pole. Similarly, the U-axis is directed towards the Galactic center, the V-axis follows the Galactic rotation, and the W-axis extends towards the North Galactic Pole. For this study, we adopted the following reference values for the solar neighborhood: the Sun’s position is (X_⊙, Y_⊙, Z_⊙) = (−8.34, 0, 0.025) kpc 29,58, with local standard of rest (LSR) velocities of (U_⊙, V_⊙, W_⊙) = (11.69, 10.16, 7.67) km s−1, Oort constants (A, B) = (16.31, −11.99) km s−1 kpc−1, and the Sun’s rotational velocity V_LSR = 231 km s−1 59. Using these values, we calculated the peculiar velocities for each star by subtracting the LSR motion, Galactic rotation, and shear effects10.

The spatial distribution of the selected O-B2 stars in the Galactic X–Y plane is shown in the left panel of Fig. 5. Due to the observational footprint of the LAMOST survey, most of these stars are situated in the outer Galactic disk. The majority of the young O-B2 stars exhibit a clustered distribution, while those at larger distances appear more dispersed, likely due to greater uncertainties in the distance estimates. Among OB associations with well-determined distances within 3 kpc, the spatial arrangement of stars clearly reflects the spiral arm structure21. In particular, we observe distinct concentrations of OB stars aligned with the Orion and Perseus arms of the Milky Way.

O-B2 stars associated with the Perseus arm
We identified a subset of O- and early B-type stars associated with the Perseus arm of the Milky Way. This selection was based on the Perseus arm model described by ref. 21. Specifically, we selected stars located within 0.5 kpc of the Perseus arm in the Galactic X–Y plane. This criterion resulted in a sample of 369 O-B2 stars.

The spatial distribution of these stars, as shown in the left panel of Fig. 5, supports their association with the Perseus arm. A detailed catalog of these stars is available online at the following URL: https://paperdata.china-vo.org/diskec/obsamp/ob2perseus.fits. This catalog offers comprehensive data for each star, including celestial coordinates, the signal-to-noise ratio of the LAMOST spectra, distance estimates, parallax values, proper motions, radial velocities, and associated uncertainties.

The right panel of Fig. 5 displays the peculiar velocity vectors of stars associated with the Perseus arm and located within 100 pc of the Galactic midplane, in the X–Y plane. These velocity patterns provide insight into the local kinematics of OB associations along the arm. A clear contrast emerges: stars near the Giant Oval Cavity—particularly those in the Cassiopeia and Auriga Peninsula regions (marked with red arrows)—exhibit coherent radial expansion away from the cavity center. In comparison, stars in other parts of the Perseus arm, such as Auriga, Gemini, and Outer Orion (blue arrows), display more irregular motions without any systematic radial expansion.

Uncertainties of the expansion and peculiar velocities
To estimate the uncertainties of the expansion and peculiar velocities of the OB stellar groups associated with the Giant Oval Cavity, we employed an MC approach based on the uncertainties of the three-dimensional positions and velocities of the individual O-B2 stars. In this method, we perturbed the measured positions and velocities by adding random noise consistent with their observational errors and recalculated the expansion and peculiar velocities across 300 realizations. The standard deviations of these resultant velocities were adopted as the uncertainty estimates: ~2 km s−1 for the expansion velocity and 3 km s−1 for the peculiar velocity.

Smoothing of vertical position and velocity profiles
To visualize the vertical position (Z) and vertical velocity (V_Z) profiles along the Perseus arm, we used the smoothfit Python package, which applies constrained optimization techniques for smooth curve fitting. Specifically, we performed one-dimensional smoothing spline fitting using smoothfit.fit1d. The fitting was conducted over the relevant range using 1000 evenly spaced evaluation points, linear basis functions (degree=1) to ensure piecewise continuity, and a regularization parameter λ=0.1 to balance between fitting accuracy and smoothness.

To assess the uncertainties of the smoothed profiles, we implemented 1000 nonparametric bootstrap resamplings of the original dataset. Each resampled dataset was smoothed using the same method, and the 1σ confidence intervals were computed from the pointwise standard deviations of the ensemble of smoothed curves.

Number of supernova events
To estimate the number of supernovae needed to create and maintain a superbubble in the Galactic disk, we modeled the bubble as an oblate spheroid with an in-plane radius of R ≈ 500 pc and a vertical height of h ≈ 100 pc, reflecting the disk’s thin structure. The volume V of the bubble is calculated as V = 4πR^2h, yielding V ≈ 3.1 × 10^63 cm^3. Our energy budget includes three components: gravitational binding energy (E_bind), turbulent pressure energy (E_turb), and radiative cooling losses (E_loss). First, E_bind is derived from the standard relation E_bind = 3/5 * G * (Σ_gas * πR^2)^2 / R. Assuming a gas surface density of Σ_g = 10 M⊙ pc−2, resulting in E_bind ≈ 6.3 × 10^51 erg. Second, E_turb is computed as E_turb = E_turb * V. We have E_turb = 1/2 * ρ_0 * δv^2, with number density n_0 = 1 cm−3 and velocity dispersion δv = 10 km s−1, giving E_turb ≈ 2.5 × 10^51 erg. Third, E_loss is calculated as E_loss = n_e^2 * Λ(T) * V * t_exp, using electron density n_e = 0.01 cm−3 (for dilute hot gas at T ~ 10^6 K), cooling function Λ(T) = 10^−22 erg cm^3 s−1, and expansion timescale t_exp = 80 Myr, yielding E_loss ≈ 7.8 × 10^52 erg. The total energy requirement is E_total ≈ 8.7 × 10^52 erg. Assuming each supernova releases E_SN ≈ 10^51 erg with a coupling efficiency of 20%, this leads to a required number of supernovae as N_SN ≈ 435.

This supernova number aligns with the expected output from a stellar population with a mass of M_* ~ 10^5 M⊙, based on a standard Salpeter initial mass function (IMF) that assumes an average of one supernova per 150 M⊙ of formed stars37. The Kennicutt–Schmidt (KS) relation45 estimates a star formation rate surface density of: Σ_SFR ≈ 2.5 × 10^−4 * (Σ_g / 1 M⊙ pc−2)^1.4 M⊙ yr−1 kpc−2. For Σ_g = 10 M⊙ pc−2 over a period of 80 Myr, this results in a stellar mass of M_* ~ 4 × 10^5 M⊙, corresponding to approximately 2600 supernovae. This value is slightly higher but remains consistent with our estimate, considering uncertainties in supernova feedback efficiency and the stochastic nature of IMF sampling.

reviewer_comments.reviewer_1:
This study utilized astrometric data from Gaia with spectroscopic data from LAMOST to obtain the 3D position and velocity maps of O-B2 stars. They measured transverse and expansion velocity of O-B2 stars near Giant oval cavity along the Perseus Arm in the Milky Way and derived that the expansion timescale of the superbubble is longer than the crossing time and shear time. Based on these estimates, they proposed that the superbubble is expanding in a quasi-stationary configuration, unlike smaller structures such as the Local Bubble.

This work has combined new astrometric and spectroscopic data to give insights into the velocity distributions of O-B2 stars near the Giant Oval Cavity, which is novel. However, all the estimates quoted lack uncertainties, and thus it is difficult to judge whether the results are significant. Furthermore, the scientific significance and potential impact to the field and related field are insufficiently justified. Finally, the physical picture of quasi-stationary expansion is based on the velocity measurement at the present day and may not be generally applicable (see Major Comments below). The manuscript needs to be improved with more quantitative analyses, and the comments below needs to be addressed before the manuscript could be considered for publication in Nature Communications.

Major comments:
1. As mentioned above, all estimated velocities lack measurement uncertainties, making it difficult to assess the significance of the results. Specifically, there are no uncertainty estimates for the expansion velocity and peculiar velocity of the O-B2 stars around the Giant Oval Cavity as well as the estimation of the relevant timescales. In Figure 2, it is unclear how the smoothed velocity profiles in the bottom panel are derived, and no error bars are provided.
2. The scientific significance of this study and potential impact of this and related fields are not sufficiently discussed. How has the study helped to improve understanding of the shaping of star forming regions by stellar feedback (regarding triggered star formation? filament formation? superbubble formation)? What key questions have the study addressed (what has been validated/invalidated)? Are the results expected or surprising (e.g., by comparing with theoretical works)? The proposed physical picture regarding the quasi-stationary expansion is vague, and it is unclear quantitatively what we could learn from such a system (e.g., estimates of injected energy required? Comparisons with inputs provided by the currently observed O-B2 stars?).
3. The primary conclusion of this study, which is the slowly expanding nature of the superbubble, is based on the velocity measurements and timescale estimates *at the present day*. However, the expansion velocity of the superbubble is likely not a constant, and the observed value at the present today could significantly underestimate the expansion velocity at earlier times. Assuming the expansion velocity was higher by a factor of a few at early phases, the expansion timescale would be shorter than the crossing and shear timescales, in which case stellar feedback would be dominant and no quasi-stationary expansion is required. In other words, this fashion of slow expansion is probably relevant only at later stages of superbubble evolution but likely not applicable throughout its expansion history. Therefore, there are not necessarily two diverse evolutionary pathways for smaller and larger bubbles; their evolutionary history could be fundamentally similar but just have evolved to different stages.

Minor comments:
1. In the Abstract, it is said that “supernovae from triggered star formation at the bubble’s edge may provide additional energy to maintain this equilibrium.” However, insufficient discussion and evidences are provided to support this conjecture.
2. In Figure 1, it is unclear what the grayscale background and contours represent.
3. In the 2nd to last paragraph in the Main Text, it is mentioned: “Sequentially triggered star formation, driven by successive supernova events, appears to be a key mechanism fueling the cavity’s expansion.” It is insufficiently described why triggered star formation is needed for the cavity’s expansion.
reviewer_comments.reviewer_2:
Chen et al. combine data on young stars in the relatively nearby Perseus Arm of the Galaxy contained in two large-scale surveys conducted by the Gaia and LAMOST instruments, respectively. They find evidence for a coherent structure in the stellar phase space data, namely two groups of stars, Cassiopeia and Auriga Peninsula which are both located towards the periphery of the "Giant oval cavity", identified in dust data, and which seem to have similar, but oppositely directed systematic expansion velocities away from the centre of this cavity.

I found the work to be somewhat interesting; with some further refinement of the text and some more details (as described below), I may be in a position to recommend the draft article for publication.

A first, overarching point is the following: the authors frame their work as the discovery of a `superbubble'; I find this usage somewhat problematic: it seems to me that the authors have found a structure in the O-B2 star phase space distribution that is, very plausibly, *related* to a superbubble identified in dust data, but it should not be identified with the superbubble. In other words, a superbubble, while related to concentrated and somewhat sustained star formation activity, is an ISM structure, not a stellar structure. In particular, I would generally take a superbubble to imply a region of high temperature, high pressure, and largely ionised gas bounded by cooler and denser, perhaps largely neutral, ISM gas. So for instance, it would sit better with me that the title were something more like "A large, long-lived, slowly-expanding stellar structure associated with a superbubble..." or similar.

Following from this point, one gets a strong visual impression from figure 1 that the Cassiopeia and Auriga Peninsula stellar groups are located at the edge of the Giant oval cavity, but how much of this apparent association is due to judicious choice of the grey scale of the dust contours? [I think the authors should define the grey scale.]

Further on this point, if I understand correctly, the stars in the Auriga peninsula and Cassiopeia groups are up to ~20 Myr, similar to the claimed expansion time of the superbubble. reviewer_comments.reviewer_3:
This paper uses Gaia-identified O-B2 stars to characterize expansion motions within a large super-bubble across one of the spiral arms of our Galaxy, a structure previously identified by Vergely et al 2022 using dust extinction maps. Based on these motions, the authors argue that this is a long-lived structure capable of surviving erosion through shear or other competing processes. They favor an explanation in which supernovae, themselves the result of star formation triggered at the edges of the super-bubble, contribute to the long-term survival of this cavity.

The paper adds valuable kinematic information about the velocity of matter in the bubble walls as inferred from the space motions of massive stars. However, we identify several issues with its central assertion.

1. The crux of the argument is that the expansion timescale is much larger than the shearing timescale. The authors estimate an expansion timescale as d/v where d is the size of the bubble and v is the expansion velocity as measured from O and B stars. However, if the current structure is the product of expansion from a significantly smaller size, then it is very likely to have decelerated to its current velocity. To argue this point on physical grounds, it would be necessary to present a physically motivated expansion law that accounts for the current and past state of the structure -- for instance, the fact that the expansion velocity is slow enough for the motion to be highly radiative, and that it is larger than the scale height of the gaseous disk. Any assertion that it is older than the shear timescale should take this history into account.

2. To fully explore the scenario in which the cavity is cleared, and kept clear, by supernovae associated with its formation, it would be necessary to evaluate how many such events are required to create its current expansion, including phenomena like the release of internal pressure when a super-bubble blows out of the gaseous disk. This would need to be compared to the plausible gas and star formation environment of the region, which one expects (on kiloparsec scales) to follow the Kennicutt-Schmidt relation.

3. The paper is incomplete without a fair evaluation of alternative scenarios. For instance, the cavity could be a purely gravitational structure, e.g., an unusually empty inter-arm region. Or, it could be related to the Parker instability. In either case, OB stars would be working within an existing under-density; it would then be easier to clear, and this may have happened more recently. The spatial correlation between OB stars and the cavity walls does not, in itself, implicate them in forming the entire structure.

Because little evidence is provided for the authors' preferred interpretation, we judge that the paper is not acceptable in its current form.

A few additional points and questions may be useful for a future version:
4. What are the uncertainties of the quoted velocities and expansion times?
5. What other signatures should accompany the structure, if it has indeed been created by supernovae? A few possibilities come to mind. There may be a giant chimney structure left behind by the blowout of the driving super-bubble. Other signatures of the driving pressure may also be identifiable. Or, there may exist a noticeable age gradient of stars whose main sequence lifetimes match the past history of the structure. The lack of such signatures may be important future constraints.
6. Are similar expansion features identifiable in other stellar structures, such as the Auriga Peninsula or the Gemini cluster?

peer_review_rounds.author_response:
Response to Reviewers
We express profound gratitude to the reviewers for their expert analysis and substantive
recommendations, which have enhanced the rigor and presentation of this study. Each
scholarly concern raised has been methodically incorporated through systematic
revisions to the manuscript. All modifications responding to the reviewers' observations
appear in blue highlighting to facilitate editorial evaluation, accompanied by detailed
rationales in this response document.
Reviewer #1 (Remarks to the Author):
Major comments:
1. As mentioned above, all estimated velocities lack measurement uncertainties, making it
difficult to assess the significance of the results. Specifically, there are no uncertainty estimates
for the expansion velocity and peculiar velocity of the O-B2 stars around the Giant Oval Cavity
as well as the estimation of the relevant timescales. In Figure 2, it is unclear how the smoothed
velocity profiles in the bottom panel are derived, and no error bars are provided.
Reply: In our study, both the three-dimensional positions and velocities of the stars
include inherent measurement errors. The uncertainties in distance arise from the
propagation of Gaia's parallax errors, while the velocity uncertainties are based on Gaia
proper motion errors combined with line-of-sight velocity errors obtained from
LAMOST spectra. To estimate the uncertainties in radial velocities, we employed a
Monte Carlo method. Using the spectral uncertainties reported by LAMOST, we added
normally distributed noise to the flux values according to their respective errors,
recalculated the radial velocities 100 times, and derived the standard deviation of the
results as the radial velocity uncertainty. Building on the full set of three-dimensional
positions and velocities, along with their associated uncertainties, we then applied a
Monte Carlo approach to estimate the uncertainties in both the expansion velocity and
the peculiar velocity of the OB groups associated with the Giant Oval Cavity. In this
process, the positions and velocities were perturbed with random noise consistent with
their measurement errors, and the expansion and peculiar velocities were recalculated
over 300 realizations. The standard deviations from these results provided the
uncertainty estimates, yielding approximately 2 km\,s$^{-1}$ for the expansion velocity
and 3 km\,s$^{-1}$ for the peculiar velocity. These methodological details and results are
now explicitly stated in the revised manuscript (Section Methods, Pages 19 - 21).
Regarding the timescale estimation, we used a characteristic size of 1 kpc for the cavity
to derive an order-of-magnitude estimate of the expansion timescale. Since this
calculation was intended as a rough approximation to assess the general evolutionary
timescale, we did not compute a formal uncertainty.
For Figure 2, we have updated the Figure to include error bars representing the
uncertainties in both position and velocity for each data point. Furthermore, we have
clarified in the revised manuscript (Section Methods, Page 21) how the smoothed velocity
and position profiles were generated. Specifically, we employed the \texttt{smoothfit}
Python package, which uses a constrained optimization method to fit smooth curves to
the vertical position ($Z$) and vertical velocity ($V_Z$) as functions of the transformed
coordinate $X'$.
2. The scientific significance of this study and potential impact of this and related fields are not
sufficiently discussed. How has the study helped to improve understanding of the shaping of
star forming regions by stellar feedback (regarding triggered star formation? filament
formation? superbubble formation)? What key questions have the study addressed (what has
been validated/invalidated)? Are the results expected or surprising (e.g., by comparing with
theoretical works)? The proposed physical picture regarding the quasi-stationary expansion is
vague, and it is unclear quantitatively what we could learn from such a system (e.g., estimates
of injected energy required? Comparisons with inputs provided by the currently observed O-
B2 stars?).
Reply: We thank the referee for emphasizing the importance of clearly articulating the
broader scientific significance of our study. Our work is motivated by the need to better
understand the origins and evolution of superbubbles in disk galaxies, a topic recently
highlighted by JWST observations revealing the widespread presence of superbubbles,
for example in NGC 628. The Giant Oval Cavity offers a particularly valuable case study,
as it likely represents a local analogue of the Phantom bubbles observed in external
galaxies. Being one of the most remarkable structures linked to stellar feedback in the
Solar vicinity, it provides a rare opportunity to investigate superbubble formation and
evolution in detail, thanks to the availability of precise astrometric and kinematic data
from Gaia and LAMOST.
Our analysis reveals that the young stellar groups associated with the Giant Oval
Cavity exhibit coherent velocity structures, indicating that their dynamics have been
influenced by feedback-driven outflows. The motions of the Cassiopeia and Auriga
Peninsula stellar groups suggest that they formed along a large-scale molecular filament,
which was subsequently fragmented and reshaped by stellar feedback. These results
illustrate how feedback mechanisms not only regulate star formation but also redistribute
gas and stars on large scales, thereby shaping the structure of the ISM.
A key finding of our study is the very slow present-day expansion velocity of the
cavity, measured to be approximately 6.2 km\,s$^{-1}$. Measuring the expansion velocity
of a superbubble with full three-dimensional positional and velocity information is
extremely challenging given the technological limits, and to our knowledge, this is the
first superbubble beyond the Local Bubble for which such a measurement has been
achieved. Despite being nearly five times larger than the Local Bubble, the Giant Oval
Cavity expands at a similar rate, implying an evolutionary timescale of about 80 Myr.
This finding challenges theoretical models that predict rapid disruption of large-scale
structures by Galactic shear and supports the idea that feedback-driven superbubbles
can maintain coherence over significantly longer periods than previously assumed. These
observations provide an important framework for interpreting the Phantom bubbles
identified by JWST in external galaxies, where direct kinematic information is not
available. Moreover, the size distribution of the JWST-detected bubbles shows a
secondary peak and a trailing extension at large radii, features that become more
prominent at greater galactocentric distances. However, the underlying physical
processes behind these distributions remain poorly constrained due to observational
limitations. The Giant Oval Cavity, together with the Local Bubble, serves as a rare,
kinematically resolved benchmark for advancing our understanding of superbubble
formation and evolution.
The observed slow expansion suggests that the cavity is currently in a late stage of
evolution, where feedback energy input is balanced by radiative cooling and Galactic
shear. This finding supports scenarios where superbubbles gradually decelerate over
time. To provide a quantitative context, we applied the superbubble model of Weaver et
al. (1977), which predicts that under constant stellar wind energy injection, a bubble with
a radius of 500 pc would require approximately 130 Myr to form. If supernova energy
inputs are included, the formation timescale would be shorter. Based on our estimates,
sustaining the Giant Oval Cavity would require an energy input equivalent to roughly
400 supernovae, assuming a 20\% energy coupling efficiency. This is consistent with the
expected output of a stellar population with a total mass of order $10^5\,M_{\odot}$.
In summary, our study addresses a key question in ISM research: how feedback-
driven structures can survive against disruptive processes like Galactic shear. By
demonstrating that a coherent superbubble can persist for approximately 80 Myr, we
provide crucial insights into the timescales and energy requirements of superbubble
evolution. This has direct relevance for interpreting observations of superbubbles in
other galaxies, especially where three-dimensional kinematic data are unavailable.
The revised manuscript now explicitly discusses these broader implications, incorporates
energy budget estimates, and compares our results with theoretical predictions.
3. The primary conclusion of this study, which is the slowly expanding nature of the
superbubble, is based on the velocity measurements and timescale estimates *at the present
day*. However, the expansion velocity of the superbubble is likely not a constant, and the
observed value at the present today could significantly underestimate the expansion velocity at
earlier times. Assuming the expansion velocity was higher by a factor of a few at early phases,
the expansion timescale would be shorter than the crossing and shear timescales, in which case
stellar feedback would be dominant and no quasi-stationary expansion is required. In other
words, this fashion of slow expansion is probably relevant only at later stages of superbubble
evolution but likely not applicable throughout its expansion history. Therefore, there are not
necessarily two diverse evolutionary pathways for smaller and larger bubbles; their
evolutionary history could be fundamentally similar but just have evolved to different stages.
Reply: We thank the referee for the thoughtful and constructive comment regarding the
time dependence of the superbubble’s expansion velocity. In response, we have revised
the manuscript to clearly state that the currently observed expansion velocity (~6.2 km/s)
represents a late-stage value and likely underestimates the velocity during earlier phases
of evolution.
Superbubbles are expected to decelerate over time due to radiative energy losses and
interactions with the ambient interstellar medium. We now incorporate in the revised
text that the expansion velocity was likely higher in the past—potentially in the range of
20–30 km/s, as proposed by Weaver et al. (1977). To better estimate the dynamical age,
we adopt a time-averaged expansion velocity of approximately 12.5 km/s. Using this value,
we derive a dynamical timescale of roughly 40 Myr, which remains longer than the
estimated Galactic shear timescale of about 30 Myr. Furthermore, we have incorporated
a physically motivated expansion model based on the framework of Weaver et al. (1977).
Applying this model with representative parameters, we find that a superbubble would
require approximately 130 Myr to reach a radius of 500 pc, slightly longer than our
earlier simple estimate based on R/v. However, the Weaver solution assumes a continuous
energy input from stellar winds, and if multiple supernovae contribute, as likely occurred,
the effective energy injection rate would be higher, thereby reducing the timescale
accordingly.
We have also revised the conclusions to emphasize that the present-day dynamics of
the Giant Oval Cavity do not exclude a faster early expansion phase. Instead, we interpret
its current properties as the result of an evolutionary sequence in which feedback-driven
expansion gradually slows over time due to radiative cooling and Galactic shear. This
framework suggests that the Giant Oval Cavity and structures such as the Local Bubble
represent different stages along a continuous evolutionary path, rather than arising from
fundamentally distinct formation mechanisms. To reflect this understanding, we have
removed prior references to “diverse” evolutionary pathways and now present the Giant
Oval Cavity as a mature superbubble where feedback and shear are approximately
balanced.
Minor comments:
1. In the Abstract, it is said that “supernovae from triggered star formation at the bubble’s edge
may provide additional energy to maintain this equilibrium.” However, insufficient discussion
and evidences are provided to support this conjecture.
Reply: In the revised manuscript, we provide additional context to support the suggestion
that triggered star formation may contribute to sustaining the cavity’s expansion. Using
the superbubble evolution framework from Weaver et al. (1977), we estimate that a
bubble driven solely by stellar winds would require ~130 Myr to reach its current radius
of 500 pc. This timescale exceeds our earlier 80 Myr estimate based on the simple ratio of
radius to velocity (𝑅/𝑣). However, the Weaver model assumes continuous energy input
from winds, whereas the inclusion of supernova energy from subsequent stellar
generations would enhance the total energy injection rate. For instance, we calculate that
the cavity’s energy budget corresponds to ~400 SNe (assuming 20\% energy coupling
efficiency).
2. In Figure 1, it is unclear what the grayscale background and contours represent.
Reply: We thank the referee for noting the ambiguity. The caption of Figure 1 has been
revised to explicitly define the grayscale background and contours.
3. In the 2nd to last paragraph in the Main Text, it is mentioned: “Sequentially triggered star
formation, driven by successive supernova events, appears to be a key mechanism fueling the
cavity’s expansion.” It is insufficiently described why triggered star formation is needed for
the cavity’s expansion.
Reply: We have expanded our discussion to clarify the importance of triggered star
formation. The revised text explains that the cavity’s sustained growth relies on a
feedback cycle: Early supernovae from the progenitor OB stars evacuate gas to form the
cavity, while subsequent shockwaves compress nearby molecular clouds, triggering new
star formation. Later supernovae from these younger stars replenish energy losses,
prolonging the expansion. This cycle aligns with the observed correlation between the
cavity’s edges and ~10 Myr-old stellar clusters, which trace dense filaments along the
cavity walls and exhibit coherent velocities indicative of feedback-driven dynamics.

Reply：We thank the referee for the thoughtful and constructive comments, which have
significantly helped improve the clarity of our manuscript. We fully agree that,
traditionally, the term "superbubble" refers to a structure within the ISM—specifically,
a cavity filled with hot, low-density gas bounded by cooler, denser material—rather than
to the associated stellar populations. In response, we have revised the manuscript to
clearly distinguish between these elements. Throughout the text, we now define the Giant
Oval Cavity as an ISM structure, originally identified through three-dimensional dust
maps by Vergely et al. (2022), with its boundary determined by enhanced dust density.
In contrast, the Cassiopeia and Auriga Peninsula stellar groups are described as young
stellar populations whose formation and kinematics have been shaped by feedback from
this cavity. It is generally very challenging to obtain the full three-dimensional position
and velocity information for gas and dust in the ISM. Therefore, young stars and stellar
associations are often used as tracers of the gas structure and kinematics, as in many
studies such as Alves et al. (2020) and Zucker et al. (2022), etc.. In our case, we first
observed that, in the XY plane, the Cassiopeia and Auriga Peninsula groups are spatially
distributed along the boundary (with larger dust density) of the Giant Oval Cavity.
Furthermore, they share a common transverse (peculiar) motion relative to the cavity,
and exhibit outward radial velocities indicative of expansion. In the vertical direction, we
observe that the Cassiopeia, Perseus, and Auriga Peninsula groups form an arc-like
structure with clear signatures of vertical expansion. In contrast, other OB groups located
in the Perseus arm, such as Auriga, Gemini, and Outer Orion, do not exhibit similar
kinematic trends. Based on these observations, we conclude that the Cassiopeia, Perseus,
and Auriga Peninsula stellar groups exhibit positions and kinematics consistent with
feedback-driven expansion from the Giant Oval Cavity, suggesting a physical link
between the ISM structure and the stellar populations. Thus, using the kinematic
properties of these stellar groups to trace the dynamics of the Giant Oval Cavity is, in our
view, a reasonable and justifiable approach. To address the referee’s concern about
Figure 1, we have updated its caption to explicitly define the grayscale and contour levels.
The boundary of the cavity was determined using a low extinction threshold (0.005 to 0.01
mag/pc), highlighting a region of exceptionally low dust content. While the apparent
spatial and kinematical coincidence between the stellar groups and the cavity boundary
is striking, the boundary reflects a real physical structure characterized by significant
dust depletion, supporting the association between the ISM cavity and the young stellar
groups.
Regarding the dynamics of the stellar groups, we clarify that we are not proposing
that the Cassiopeia and Auriga Peninsula stars were ejected from the center of the cavity.
The O-B2 stars we selected are generally younger than ~10 Myr. Our working hypothesis
is that a pre-existing, elongated dense gas filament passed through the expanding
superbubble, where star formation was triggered along its path. The resulting stellar
kinematics were then influenced by local feedback processes associated with the
superbubble’s expansion, rather than by a ballistic launch from the cavity center.
We also agree that the expansion of the superbubble boundary is not expected to
have occurred at a constant velocity. In response to this and similar concerns raised by
other referees, we have revised the manuscript to clarify that the currently observed
expansion velocity of approximately 6.2 km\,s$^{-1}$ likely reflects a late-stage value,
and underestimates the velocity at earlier phases of evolution. Superbubbles are expected
to decelerate over time due to radiative energy losses and interactions with the
surrounding ISM. We now incorporate estimates of earlier expansion velocities (e.g., 20–
30 km\,s$^{-1}$; Weaver et al. 1977) and demonstrate that, even when adopting a time-
averaged velocity, the inferred dynamical age of approximately 40 Myr remains
consistent with our conclusions. Accordingly, we have revised the manuscript to present
the Giant Oval Cavity as a mature superbubble in a late evolutionary phase, where its
expansion is now regulated by Galactic shear and radiative cooling. Although our study
primarily relies on optical observations of stars, the scientific focus is on the connection
between stellar feedback and superbubble dynamics. Recent JWST observations
revealing the widespread presence of superbubbles in galaxies such as NGC 628 have
renewed interest in understanding the formation and evolution of these structures.
However, in external galaxies, the absence of detailed kinematic information limits our
ability to constrain their physical properties. In contrast, the Solar neighborhood, with
the precise astrometry provided by Gaia, offers a unique opportunity to study these
processes in detail. To our knowledge, this work represents the first measurement of the
expansion velocity for a superbubble beyond the Local Bubble. This forms the primary
motivation for our study. Our contribution is to identify the Giant Oval Cavity as a slowly
expanding structure and to establish its connection to the broader framework of
feedback-regulated ISM evolution in disk galaxies. Understanding how superbubbles
form, evolve, and interact with their environment is a critical component of the larger
picture of galaxy evolution across cosmic time.

(via the Python package smoothfit), employing linear basis functions and a regularization
parameter \lambda=0.1 to balance smoothness and fidelity to the data. To quantify

measurements and a shaded confidence band around the smoothed velocity profile,
reinforcing the significance of the gradient.

boundary is unlikely to arise by chance. We propose that the cavity exists in a quasi-
stationary state, where feedback energy from sequential supernovae balances radiative
losses and shear forces. This equilibrium is consistent with the cavity’s slow present-day

assuming a constant expansion velocity oversimplifies the bubble’s dynamical history,
especially given the likelihood of deceleration due to radiative cooling and interaction
with the ambient interstellar medium. To address this, we have revised the manuscript
to incorporate a physically motivated expansion model. Specifically, we adopt the
framework of Weaver et al. (1977), which describes the evolution of a superbubble driven
by stellar winds. This model provides a time-dependent scaling for the bubble’s radius
during the adiabatic phase:
R(t) = 27 n_0^{-1/5} L_{36}^{1/5} t_6^{3/5} pc,
where n_0 is the ambient density in cm^{-3}, L_{36} is the wind luminosity in units of

supernovae are needed to form and sustain the cavity, considering these combined effects.

2002; Zucker et al. 2022), we estimate that the formation of the larger cavity would
require roughly 25 times more supernovae, or approximately 500 events. This
independent estimate is in good agreement with our detailed calculation.

cavity could be a purely gravitational structure, e.g., an unusually empty inter-arm region. Or,

paper is not acceptable in its current form.
Reply: We thank the referee for highlighting the importance of evaluating alternative
scenarios for the origin of the cavity. In the revised manuscript, we have carefully
considered the two hypotheses suggested—namely, a pre-existing inter-arm underdensity
and structures formed by Parker instability—and have provided a detailed comparison
with our preferred interpretation involving stellar feedback.
If the cavity were simply a quiescent inter-arm region, we would expect its
kinematics to follow Galactic rotation and shear patterns. However, the Cassiopeia and
Auriga Peninsula groups display radially outward velocities (v_exp ≈ 6.2 km/s) that
deviate significantly from the expected motions in a passive shear environment. Moreover,
the dust column density within the cavity (\delta A_0 < 0.005 mag/pc) is an order of
magnitude lower than that typically observed in inter-arm regions (~0.2 mag/pc; Vergely
et al. 2022), implying an initial underdensity that would be unusually extreme. The stellar
population also differs markedly: stars associated with the cavity walls are young (ages ≤
discrepancies in both kinematics and stellar ages strongly argue against a passive, pre-
existing underdensity origin.
Regarding the Parker instability scenario, theoretical models predict gas-dominated
structures characterized by undular (wavelength λ ∼ 1 kpc; Parker 1979; Rodrigues et
al. 2016). In contrast, the Giant Oval Cavity shows a smooth, elliptical morphology that
does not match these predictions. Furthermore, the cavity is defined by significant dust
evacuation and coherent vertical velocity gradients—features not typically associated
with Parker instability, which primarily organizes gas without significant feedback
signatures from young stars.

radially outward motions relative to the cavity center. Such kinematic coherence is
unlikely to arise from random star formation within a pre-existing void, which would be
expected to produce more isotropic velocity distributions. In comparison, other nearby

shear-driven kinematics, and the organized feedback-driven morphology collectively
argue against the alternatives of a pre-existing underdensity or Parker instability origin.

strong evidence that stellar feedback is the primary driver of the cavity’s formation and
ongoing evolution.

these alternative hypotheses and to clarify why stellar feedback remains the most
consistent explanation.
A few additional points and questions may be useful for a future version:
4. What are the uncertainties of the quoted velocities and expansion times?

the revised manuscript. Using the full three-dimensional positions and velocities of stars
near the Giant Oval Cavity, we applied a Monte Carlo method to quantify the
uncertainties. Specifically, each star’s position and velocity were perturbed 300 times
with Gaussian noise based on their observational errors (e.g., parallax and proper motion
uncertainties from Gaia DR3, and radial velocity uncertainties from LAMOST). The
standard deviation of these realizations gives an uncertainty of approximately 2 km/s for
the cavity’s expansion velocity and about 3 km/s for the peculiar motions of OB stars.
The expansion timescale is an order-of-magnitude calculation based on the current size
of the cavity (R∼1 kpc). We did not compute a formal error for this timescale.
5. What other signatures should accompany the structure, if it has indeed been created by
supernovae? A few possibilities come to mind. There may be a giant chimney structure left
behind by the blowout of the driving super-bubble. Other signatures of the driving pressure

sequence lifetimes match the past history of the structure. The lack of such signatures may be
important future constraints.
Reply: We fully agree with the referee that, if the cavity was formed by supernova-driven
feedback, additional signatures such as giant chimneys, thermal pressure gradients, or
stellar age gradients might be expected. However, current observational limitations make
systematic verification of these features challenging.
For vertical gas channels (chimney structures), detection is difficult. Identifying soft
X-ray emission or high-velocity H$\alpha$ filaments requires highly sensitive
spectroscopic imaging. Since the cavity lies within the Galactic disk, separating
foreground and background emissions introduces significant systematic uncertainties,
potentially obscuring such features.
Quantitative analysis of thermal pressure is also limited. Accurate determination of the
internal pressure would require multi-wavelength diagnostics combining X-ray spectral
fitting (for electron temperatures and densities) and ultraviolet absorption-line
measurements (to assess non-thermal turbulence). Investigating stellar age gradients
presents further technical challenges. Identifying feedback-triggered star formation
sequences would require precise photometric measurements and reliable extinction
corrections, typically using isochrone fitting methods. However, in high-extinction
regions of the Galactic plane, the uncertainties are significant, limiting the accuracy of
age estimates.

would provide important constraints, and we view this as a valuable direction for future
work.
6. Are similar expansion features identifiable in other stellar structures, such as the Auriga
Peninsula or the Gemini cluster?

the Auriga Peninsula or the Gemini groups. The absence of similar kinematic patterns in
these groups suggests that the Giant Oval Cavity is unique in its feedback-driven origin.

robustness of our interpretation. This collaboration led to the integration of new insights

concise and coherent picture of the formation and stability of large, stationary

revised manuscript more accessible and impactful.

anticipated. In particular, the historical aspects of the bubble's development, which
featured more prominently in the earlier draft, have been deemphasized in light of our

consequence of the dialogue with the referees, for which we are deeply grateful. We hope

Reviewer #1 (Remarks to the Author):
1. After considering possible deceleration during the evolution using the model of Weaver et
al., the estimated expansion time is adjusted to ~40 Myr. This is in fact not much longer than
the shear timescale of ~30 Myr, or could be considered comparable given that these numbers
are order-of-magnitude estimates. Since these timescales are not significantly different, this
challenges the physical picture proposed by the authors. In other words, there does not need to
be a balance between stellar feedback and shear forces, but it could well be that we are
observing the Giant Oval Cavity currently undergoing deformation/disruption due to the
Galactic shear, i.e., the Cavity does not need to be long lived.
2. There appears to be some inconsistency between the power of energy injection assumed in
the timescale estimate based on the model of Weaver et al. and that used to justify the formation
of the Giant Oval Cavity by SN explosions. The former assumes cavity formation due to
constant energy injections with a stellar wind luminosity of 10^36 erg/s. On the other hand, the
latter requires 400-500 SN explosions, which corresponds to a kinetic luminosity of ~400 SNe
x 1e51 erg / 80 Myr x 20\% ~ 2.53e39 erg/s, which is much greater than the stellar wind
luminosity assumed in the timescale estimate. Since the adopted luminosity would significantly
influence the timescale estimate, could the authors please clarify the adopted numbers and the
assumed source of energy injection for cavity formation?
Reply (combing 1 and 2): We thank the reviewer for the insightful comments, which have
prompted us to critically reassess our interpretation of the timescales involved in the
evolution of the Giant Oval Cavity. The point regarding the similarity between the
estimated expansion timescale (~40 Myr) and the galactic shear timescale (~30 Myr) is
well taken, particularly given the approximations inherent in both estimates. We agree
that this proximity in values complicates the interpretation of the cavity’s longevity and
challenges the assumption of a clear distinction between a dynamically balanced and a
transient structure.
As the reviewer rightly notes, the expansion timescale derived using the Weaver et al.
(1977) model assumes a constant energy injection rate and simplified conditions, which
may not capture the complexity of the actual environment. Given the sensitivity of such
models to assumed parameters (e.g., ambient density, efficiency of energy coupling, and
the nature of energy injection), we recognize that relying on this analytical framework to
establish the cavity’s age or stability introduces considerable uncertainty. In light of this,
we have removed the Weaver model analysis from the revised manuscript.
To provide a more physically grounded picture, we now base our interpretation on
results from numerical simulations provided by Prof. Martin Krause. These simulations
demonstrate that large cavities can enter a state of dynamical equilibrium, where their
boundaries are shaped and maintained by ongoing interactions between supernova-
driven feedback and inflowing interstellar gas. While such structures may deform or
migrate over time, the simulations show they can remain coherent and long-lived if
energy injection is sustained. This view supports the idea that the Giant Oval Cavity may
persist not because it is “young” (or “old”) but because it exists in a quasi-stationary state
maintained by feedback processes.

characterize the cavity’s stability through a comparison of relevant dynamical timescales.
We introduce the concept of a survival timescale, defined as: t_survival = l_bubble /

\sigma_v,disk is the velocity dispersion of the surrounding interstellar medium. This estimate
significantly exceeds the shear timescale (t_shear ≈ 30 Myr), indicating that the cavity is
resilient against turbulent disruption. Furthermore, the characteristic timescale between
supernova events is: t_SN ≈ 0.5 Myr (Eq. 6), which is orders of magnitude shorter than
t_survival. This ensures a continuous supply of energy capable of offsetting the effects of
shear and maintaining structural coherence.

show that superbubbles with t_SN ≪ t_survival can maintain quasi-stationary
boundaries for extended periods through a balance between feedback and inflow. We
have included these results and relevant figures (e.g., Figure 3 in the revised manuscript)
to illustrate this mechanism more clearly.
We hope this revised analysis, grounded in simulation-based evidence and dynamical
reasoning, addresses the concerns raised and provides a more robust physical
interpretation of the Giant Oval Cavity.

report except for a single, remaining point: could they please generate a greyscale numerical

publication.

in Figure 1 to quantify the dust density scale in the background map. This addition
enhances the interpretability of the figure by providing a clear reference for the dust
distribution values. In response, we have modified the figure accordingly. The bar is
positioned adjacent to the right panel of Figure 1.

1. It is not sufficient to introduce the Weaver model and state the bubble age for some choice
of parameters (e.g., L_36 = 1) without exploring which parameters match the structure as it is
currently observed -- in other words, finding which values of luminosity and age are consistent
with both the current radius and the current expansion velocity.

the effective wind luminosity.)

ratio of radius to velocity (80 Myr) stressed elsewhere. This is obviously an overestimate,
because the radial evolution within the Weaver model is R ~ t^eta with eta = 3/5. This law is
consistent with t = eta R/v = 48 Myr.

manuscript and for the detailed comments, which have led us to reconsider and refine
both our methodology and the structure of our argument. Regarding the application of
the Weaver et al. (1977) model, we acknowledge the limitations inherent in using a
simplified analytic framework without a thorough exploration of parameter space.

physically grounded and comprehensive picture based on numerical simulations. With
the assistance of Prof. Martin Krause, we now incorporate simulation results that
emphasize the role of large-scale feedback-driven structures in establishing long-lived
cavities. These simulations clarify that the size of the cavity itself plays a central role in
regulating its evolution, enabling efficient energy conversion from successive supernovae

the long-term stability of the cavity through continuous energy injection. These
arguments are now supported by recent simulations, which show that cavities with t_SN

"snowplow" expansion. The appropriate value of eta, for a circular shell undergoing
snowplow expansion within a disk, is 1/3, which suggests an age as low as 27 Myr -- comparable to the

interpretation is supported by the simulations we now include in the revised manuscript,
particularly those from Krause et al. (2019), which explicitly show blowout phases in the
evolution of similar large cavities. We have updated the text to reflect this physical
transition and its implications for the bubble’s expansion dynamics. As a result, we no
longer rely on age estimates derived from spherical or pressure-driven expansion models,
which are not appropriate once blowout has occurred.

from cooling in the bubble interior. However, spherical models of superbubbles often find that
heat lost by conduction is greater than cooling in the interior: see for instance El Badry et al
2019. When blowout has occurred, the energy lost is even greater.
Reply: We appreciate the reviewer’s observation regarding energy losses in large cavities.

significantly affect the internal energy budget of the bubble—particularly in the post-
blowout phase. However, as the reviewer notes, the impact of thermal conduction scales
with the surface area of the interface between the hot bubble and the cooler surroundings.

importance of conduction diminishes as the cavity grows. Conversely, energy loss into the
circumgalactic medium becomes more significant after blowout. This mechanism has
been addressed in the simulations by Krause et al. (2019), which we now cite and discuss
in the revised manuscript. We have also clarified that our energy budget estimates are
intended as order-of-magnitude assessments rather than precise calculations.

to the associations lining this cavity, and not characteristic of random motions elsewhere in the
disk, would strengthen the case for its existence.
Reply: We thank the reviewer for underscoring the importance of explicitly establishing
the uniqueness of the kinematic expansion signatures associated with the Giant Oval
Cavity. We have strengthened our argument by added a new panel of Figure 5, which
visually and unequivocally demonstrates the spatial correlation between coherent radial
motions and the cavity boundary. In the revised manuscript, we now explicitly describe
the velocity patterns revealed by the figure: stars in the Cassiopeia and Auriga Peninsula
groups (marked as red arrows) exhibit coherent radially outward motions aligned with
the periphery of the Giant Oval Cavity. This geometric consistency—where velocity
vectors point away from the cavity center—supports their expansion origin. Critically,
this pattern is absent in other Perseus arm groups (Auriga, Gemini, and Outer Orion;
blue arrows), whose velocity vectors show random orientations without systematic radial
alignment relative to any cavity.
